hook: The conqueror who was horrified by his own war and became a king of peace.

pages.x: Ashoka was a grandson of Chandragupta, founder of the Maurya Empire. Later Buddhist stories say he was so harsh that people called him "Ashoka the Fierce", and that he killed his brothers to take the throne at Pataliputra around 268 BC.

Around 261 BC he invaded Kalinga, a kingdom on the east coast of India. In his own words, 100,000 people were killed, 150,000 carried away, and many more died afterwards. His empire now covered almost all of India, larger than any until the British.

Seeing the slaughter, Ashoka was filled with grief. He turned to Buddhism and gave up wars of conquest. From then on he would rule by dhamma, right conduct: kindness, honesty, respect for all religions, and care for people and animals.

He had his laws and thoughts carved on rocks and tall polished pillars across the empire, in local languages, even Greek and Aramaic. In them he says he regrets Kalinga, bans killing animals for sacrifice in his capital, and orders wells dug, trees planted and hospitals built for people and animals.

One of his pillars, at Sarnath, where the Buddha first taught, was topped by four lions sitting back to back above a wheel. Today it is the national emblem of India, and the wheel, the Ashoka Chakra, sits in the middle of India's flag.

He sent Buddhist teachers to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and the Greek kingdoms of the west. His son Mahinda and his daughter Sanghamitta took Buddhism to Sri Lanka, with a cutting of the tree under which the Buddha woke up. A descendant of that tree still grows at Anuradhapura.

Ashoka turned from conqueror to a king of peace, and helped turn Buddhism from an Indian sect into a world religion. His edicts are among the oldest readable writings from India, and his lions still stand for India.
pts: Gave up war after the slaughter at Kalinga
His lions and wheel are on India's emblem and flag
